find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.title: Find Numbers with Even Number of Digits
find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.statement: Given a list of positive integers, count how many of them are written with an even number of decimal digits.
find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.details:
**Task.** You get an array of positive integers. Count the numbers whose decimal representation has an even number of digits.

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 500; 1 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[12, 345, 2, 6, 7896]` → `2`. 12 has two digits and 7896 has four; the others have an odd count.
find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.approach: One pass; for each number count its digits (divide by 10, or check ranges 10–99, 1000–9999, …) and increment a counter if the count is even.
find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.trigger: "count how many elements satisfy …" with an independent per-element test.

richest-customer-wealth.title: Richest Customer Wealth
richest-customer-wealth.statement: A grid lists, for each customer (row), the money they hold in each bank (column). Return the largest total wealth of any single customer.
richest-customer-wealth.details:
**Task.** An m × n grid `accounts` gives, for customer i (a row), the amount they keep in bank j (a column). A customer's wealth is the total across all their banks. Return the wealth of the richest customer.

**Input:** a 2-D integer array. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 50; 1 ≤ `accounts[i][j]` ≤ 100.

**Example:** `[[1,5],[7,3],[3,5]]` → `10`. The totals are 6, 10 and 8.
richest-customer-wealth.pattern_name: Running sum per row + best so far
richest-customer-wealth.approach: For each row, sum it with a running total, then update a global maximum.

element-appearing-more-than-25-in-sorted.title: Element Appearing More Than 25% In Sorted Array
element-appearing-more-than-25-in-sorted.statement: A sorted array has exactly one value that occurs in more than a quarter of the positions. Return it.
element-appearing-more-than-25-in-sorted.details:
**Task.** An array sorted in non-decreasing order contains exactly one value that fills more than 25% of its positions. Return that value.

**Input:** a sorted integer array `arr`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 10⁴; 0 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 2, 6, 6, 6, 6, 7, 10]` → `6`. It fills 4 of the 9 positions, which is more than a quarter.
element-appearing-more-than-25-in-sorted.approach: Duplicates are adjacent in sorted input, so track the length of the current run of equal values and return the value when the run exceeds n/4. (Clever version: check if a[i] == a[i + n/4].)
element-appearing-more-than-25-in-sorted.trigger: "sorted" + "appears more than …" → equal values sit together, count runs.

three-consecutive-odds.title: Three Consecutive Odds
three-consecutive-odds.statement: Return true if the array contains three odd numbers in a row.
three-consecutive-odds.details:
**Task.** Return true if somewhere in the array there are three odd numbers at consecutive positions, otherwise false.

**Input:** an integer array `arr`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 1000; 1 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 34, 3, 4, 5, 7, 23, 12]` → `true` (5, 7, 23). `[2, 6, 4, 1]` → `false`.
three-consecutive-odds.approach: Streak counter that increments on odd and resets on even; return true when it reaches 3.

remove-one-element-to-make-the-array-str.title: Remove One Element to Make the Array Strictly Increasing
remove-one-element-to-make-the-array-str.statement: Decide whether deleting exactly one element can leave the array strictly increasing.
remove-one-element-to-make-the-array-str.details:
**Task.** Remove exactly one element from the array. Can the remaining elements, in their original order, be strictly increasing? (An array that is already strictly increasing also counts: removing any one element keeps it so.)

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 1000; 1 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 10, 5, 7]` → `true`: remove 10 to get `[1, 2, 5, 7]`. `[2, 3, 1, 2]` → `false`. `[1, 1, 1]` → `false`.
remove-one-element-to-make-the-array-str.approach: Walk once counting positions where a[i] ≤ a[i−1]. More than one → false. At the single violation, check whether removing a[i−1] or a[i] fixes it by comparing with a[i−2] / a[i+1].
remove-one-element-to-make-the-array-str.trigger: "remove one element" + "strictly increasing" → scan once for the violation, decide locally.

check-if-the-sentence-is-pangram.title: Check if the Sentence Is Pangram
check-if-the-sentence-is-pangram.statement: Decide whether a lowercase sentence uses every letter of the alphabet at least once.
check-if-the-sentence-is-pangram.details:
**Task.** A sentence contains only lowercase English letters. Is every one of the 26 letters present at least once?

**Input:** a string `sentence`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 1000; lowercase letters only.

**Example:** `"thequickbrownfoxjumpsoverthelazydog"` → `true`. `"leetcode"` → `false`.
check-if-the-sentence-is-pangram.approach: Mark each letter seen in a bool[26] (or set); true iff all 26 marked.
check-if-the-sentence-is-pangram.trigger: "every letter / all characters" over a fixed alphabet.

isomorphic-strings.title: Isomorphic Strings
isomorphic-strings.statement: Two strings of equal length; decide whether the characters of the first can be replaced one-to-one to produce the second.
isomorphic-strings.details:
**Task.** Two strings `s` and `t` of equal length. Can every character of `s` be replaced by some character so that `s` becomes `t`? All occurrences of a character must get the same replacement, and two different characters may not map to the same one. A character may map to itself.

**Input:** strings `s`, `t`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 5·10⁴; `s` and `t` have the same length and contain any valid ASCII characters.

**Example:** `"egg"`, `"add"` → `true`. `"foo"`, `"bar"` → `false` (o would need to become both a and r). `"paper"`, `"title"` → `true`.
isomorphic-strings.approach: Keep two maps s→t and t→s; at each position both must agree with earlier mappings (or both be new). Equivalent: compare the "first occurrence index" patterns of both strings.
isomorphic-strings.trigger: "one-to-one mapping / same pattern" between two sequences.

word-pattern.title: Word Pattern
word-pattern.statement: Given a pattern like "abba" and a sentence of words, decide whether the words follow the pattern with a one-to-one letter↔word mapping.
word-pattern.details:
**Task.** A pattern of letters and a sentence of words. Does the sentence follow the pattern? That means the k-th letter corresponds to the k-th word, equal letters always correspond to the same word, and different letters always correspond to different words.

**Input:** a string `pattern` and a string `s` of words separated by single spaces. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ `pattern` length ≤ 300; 1 ≤ `s` length ≤ 3000; lowercase letters only; no leading or trailing spaces.

**Example:** `"abba"`, `"dog cat cat dog"` → `true`. `"abba"`, `"dog cat cat fish"` → `false`. `"aaaa"`, `"dog cat cat dog"` → `false`.
word-pattern.approach: Split the sentence; lengths must match; maintain char→word and word→char maps and reject any conflict.
word-pattern.trigger: "follows the same pattern" → bijection check with two hash maps.

unique-number-of-occurrences.title: Unique Number of Occurrences
unique-number-of-occurrences.statement: Return true if no two distinct values in the array occur the same number of times.
unique-number-of-occurrences.details:
**Task.** Look at how many times each distinct value occurs in the array. Return true if no two distinct values occur the same number of times.

**Input:** an integer array `arr`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 1000; −1000 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 3]` → `true` (1 occurs 3 times, 2 occurs twice, 3 once). `[1, 2]` → `false` (both occur once).
unique-number-of-occurrences.pattern_name: Count, then check the counts are distinct
unique-number-of-occurrences.approach: Frequency map; insert every count into a set; true iff the set size equals the number of distinct values.
unique-number-of-occurrences.trigger: question is about the counts themselves → count first, then reason about counts.

how-many-numbers-are-smaller-than-the-cu.title: How Many Numbers Are Smaller Than the Current Number
how-many-numbers-are-smaller-than-the-cu.statement: For each element, report how many other elements are strictly smaller. Values are between 0 and 100.
how-many-numbers-are-smaller-than-the-cu.details:
**Task.** For every position i, count the positions j with `nums[j] < nums[i]`. Return those counts as an array, in the original order.

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** an integer array of the same length.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 500; 0 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 100.

**Example:** `[8, 1, 2, 2, 3]` → `[4, 0, 1, 1, 3]`. Four values are below 8; none are below 1; one (the 1) is below each 2.
how-many-numbers-are-smaller-than-the-cu.approach: Values are small → count each value, take a running prefix of counts; answer for x is the total count of values < x.
how-many-numbers-are-smaller-than-the-cu.trigger: small value range (0..100) → counting array instead of sorting or nested loops.

check-if-n-and-its-double-exist.title: Check If N and Its Double Exist
check-if-n-and-its-double-exist.statement: Decide whether the array contains two different positions holding x and 2x.
check-if-n-and-its-double-exist.details:
**Task.** Are there two different indices i ≠ j such that `arr[i]` is exactly twice `arr[j]`?

**Input:** an integer array `arr`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 500; −1000 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[10, 2, 5, 3]` → `true` (10 = 2 × 5). `[3, 1, 7, 11]` → `false`. `[0, 0]` → `true`, but `[0]` alone could never pair with itself.
check-if-n-and-its-double-exist.approach: Walk once with a set; for each x check whether 2x or x/2 (when x is even) was seen before, then insert x.
check-if-n-and-its-double-exist.trigger: "exists i ≠ j with a relation between a[i] and a[j]" on unsorted data → hash set.

backspace-string-compare.title: Backspace String Compare
backspace-string-compare.statement: Two strings where '#' means backspace; decide whether they produce the same text.
backspace-string-compare.details:
**Task.** Each string is a sequence of keystrokes typed into an empty editor, where `#` is a backspace. Backspace on an empty editor does nothing. Do the two strings leave the same text?

**Input:** strings `s`, `t`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ lengths ≤ 200; lowercase letters and `#` only. Follow-up: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**Example:** `"ab#c"`, `"ad#c"` → `true` (both give `"ac"`). `"a##c"`, `"#a#c"` → `true` (both give `"c"`). `"a#c"`, `"b"` → `false`.
backspace-string-compare.pattern_name: Two pointers from the back (or a stack)
backspace-string-compare.approach: A stack builds each final string in O(n) space. For O(1): walk both strings from the end, skipping characters cancelled by pending backspaces, comparing the next real characters.
backspace-string-compare.trigger: "backspace / undo" → stack; "O(1) space" follow-up → pointers from the end.

is-subsequence.title: Is Subsequence
is-subsequence.statement: Decide whether s can be obtained from t by deleting some characters without reordering.
is-subsequence.details:
**Task.** Can `s` be obtained from `t` by deleting zero or more characters of `t` without changing the order of the rest?

**Input:** strings `s`, `t`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 0 ≤ `s` length ≤ 100; 0 ≤ `t` length ≤ 10⁴; lowercase letters only. Follow-up: billions of different `s` strings against the same `t`.

**Example:** `"abc"`, `"ahbgdc"` → `true`. `"axc"`, `"ahbgdc"` → `false`.
is-subsequence.pattern_name: Two pointers moving in the same direction
is-subsequence.approach: Pointer i in s, j in t; advance j always, advance i when s[i] == t[j]; true if i reaches the end of s.
is-subsequence.trigger: "subsequence check" between two sequences → greedy same-direction pointers.

minimum-difference-between-highest-and-l.title: Minimum Difference Between Highest and Lowest of K Scores
minimum-difference-between-highest-and-l.statement: Pick k scores so that the gap between the largest and smallest picked is as small as possible.
minimum-difference-between-highest-and-l.details:
**Task.** Choose any k students' scores from the array. Make the difference between the highest and lowest chosen score as small as possible, and return that difference.

**Input:** an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ k ≤ length ≤ 1000; 0 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[9, 4, 1, 7]`, k = 2 → `2`. Choosing 9 and 7 gives 2, and no pair is closer. `[90]`, k = 1 → `0`.
minimum-difference-between-highest-and-l.approach: Sort; the best k always form a contiguous block in sorted order; answer = min over i of a[i+k−1] − a[i].
minimum-difference-between-highest-and-l.trigger: "choose k elements minimising max − min" → sort, then the choice is a window.

long-pressed-name.title: Long Pressed Name
long-pressed-name.statement: A friend typed a name, but some keys may have been held down and repeated. Decide whether the typed text could come from the name.
long-pressed-name.details:
**Task.** Your friend typed their name, but some keys may have been held down, so a character may appear one or more extra times in a row. Could `typed` be the result of typing `name` this way?

**Input:** strings `name`, `typed`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ lengths ≤ 1000; lowercase letters only.

**Example:** `"alex"`, `"aaleex"` → `true`. `"saeed"`, `"ssaaedd"` → `false`: the second e is missing, and the extra d does not belong.
long-pressed-name.approach: Pointer i in name, j in typed; if characters match advance both; else if typed[j] repeats typed[j−1] advance j; else false. At the end i must reach the end of name.
long-pressed-name.trigger: comparing two sequences where one may contain extra repeats → two forward pointers.

sum-of-all-odd-length-subarrays.title: Sum of All Odd Length Subarrays
sum-of-all-odd-length-subarrays.statement: Add up the sums of every contiguous subarray whose length is odd.
sum-of-all-odd-length-subarrays.details:
**Task.** Consider every contiguous subarray whose length is odd (1, 3, 5, …). Return the sum of all their sums.

**Input:** an integer array `arr`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 100; 1 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 1000. Follow-up: O(n).

**Example:** `[1, 4, 2, 5, 3]` → `58`. The length-1 subarrays add up to 15. The length-3 ones are 7, 11 and 10, so 28. The length-5 one is 15. 15 + 28 + 15 = 58.
sum-of-all-odd-length-subarrays.approach: With prefix sums, each odd-length subarray sum is O(1) → O(n²) total. O(n) trick: element i appears in ((i+1)(n−i)+1)/2 odd-length subarrays; sum a[i] × that count.
sum-of-all-odd-length-subarrays.trigger: "sum over many subarrays" → prefix sums, or count how many subarrays each element belongs to.

find-the-pivot-integer.title: Find the Pivot Integer
find-the-pivot-integer.statement: Find x in 1..n such that 1 + … + x equals x + … + n, or −1.
find-the-pivot-integer.details:
**Task.** Given a positive integer n, find the integer x with 1 ≤ x ≤ n such that the sum 1 + 2 + … + x equals the sum x + (x+1) + … + n. Return x, or −1 if there is none. There is at most one such x.

**Input:** an integer `n`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `n = 8` → `6` (1+…+6 = 21 = 6+7+8). `n = 1` → `1`. `n = 4` → `-1`.
find-the-pivot-integer.approach: Left = x(x+1)/2, right = total − left + x; scan x, or solve x² = n(n+1)/2 directly.
find-the-pivot-integer.trigger: "sum on the left equals sum on the right" → prefix sum + total (Pivot Index).

maximum-score-after-splitting-a-string.title: Maximum Score After Splitting a String
maximum-score-after-splitting-a-string.statement: Split a binary string into two non-empty parts; score = zeros in the left part + ones in the right part. Return the best score.
maximum-score-after-splitting-a-string.details:
**Task.** A string of 0s and 1s is cut into a non-empty left part and a non-empty right part. The score is the number of 0s in the left part plus the number of 1s in the right part. Return the best score over all possible cuts.

**Input:** a binary string `s`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 500.

**Example:** `"011101"` → `5`. Cutting after the first character gives `"0"` + `"11101"`: one zero plus four ones. `"00111"` → `5`.
maximum-score-after-splitting-a-string.approach: Count all ones first; walk split points keeping zeros-so-far and ones-so-far; score = zerosLeft + (totalOnes − onesLeft). Keep both parts non-empty.
maximum-score-after-splitting-a-string.trigger: "split into left and right, score each side" → one running prefix and one total.

number-of-ways-to-split-array.title: Number of Ways to Split Array
number-of-ways-to-split-array.statement: Count split points where the sum of the left part is at least the sum of the right part (both parts non-empty).
number-of-ways-to-split-array.details:
**Task.** A split at index i (0 ≤ i < n − 1) divides the array into `nums[0..i]` and `nums[i+1..n−1]`, so both parts are non-empty. It is valid when the left part's sum is at least the right part's sum. Count the valid splits.

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 10⁵; −10⁵ ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[10, 4, -8, 7]` → `2`. The splits give 10 vs 3 (valid), 14 vs −1 (valid) and 6 vs 7 (not valid).
number-of-ways-to-split-array.pattern_name: Prefix sum + total, in long long
number-of-ways-to-split-array.approach: Total first; running left sum; at each split i (0..n−2) check left ≥ total − left. Sums up to 10¹⁰ → long long.
number-of-ways-to-split-array.trigger: "left sum vs right sum at every split" → running prefix + total.

maximum-number-of-balloons.title: Maximum Number of Balloons
maximum-number-of-balloons.statement: Using each letter of a text at most once, how many copies of the word "balloon" can be formed?
maximum-number-of-balloons.details:
**Task.** You may use each character of `text` at most once. How many complete copies of the word `"balloon"` can you form?

**Input:** a string `text`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 10⁴; lowercase letters only.

**Example:** `"nlaebolko"` → `1`. `"loonbalxballpoon"` → `2`. `"leetcode"` → `0`.
maximum-number-of-balloons.approach: Count letters of the text; answer = min(b, a, l/2, o/2, n).
maximum-number-of-balloons.trigger: "how many times can a word be built from these letters" → counts divided by the word's own counts.

grumpy-bookstore-owner.title: Grumpy Bookstore Owner
grumpy-bookstore-owner.statement: Customers arrive each minute; on grumpy minutes they leave unsatisfied. The owner can stay calm for one block of m consecutive minutes. Maximise satisfied customers.
grumpy-bookstore-owner.details:
**Task.** A shop is open for n minutes. In minute i, `customers[i]` people come in. If `grumpy[i]` is 1 the owner is grumpy that minute and those customers leave unsatisfied; otherwise they are satisfied. Once, the owner can force themselves to stay calm for `minutes` consecutive minutes. Return the maximum number of satisfied customers.

**Input:** integer arrays `customers` and `grumpy` of length n, and an integer `minutes`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ minutes ≤ n ≤ 2·10⁴; 0 ≤ `customers[i]` ≤ 1000; `grumpy[i]` is 0 or 1.

**Example:** `customers = [1,0,1,2,1,1,7,5]`, `grumpy = [0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1]`, minutes = 3 → `16`. Staying calm for the last three minutes adds 1 + 5 to the 10 who were already satisfied.
grumpy-bookstore-owner.approach: Base = customers on non-grumpy minutes. Slide a window of size m summing customers on grumpy minutes inside it (the extra gained); answer = base + max window.
grumpy-bookstore-owner.trigger: "choose one block of exactly m consecutive minutes" → fixed window.

substrings-of-size-three-with-distinct-c.title: Substrings of Size Three with Distinct Characters
substrings-of-size-three-with-distinct-c.statement: Count the length-3 substrings whose three characters are all different.
substrings-of-size-three-with-distinct-c.details:
**Task.** Count the substrings of length exactly 3 in which all three characters are different. The same substring counts each time it occurs.

**Input:** a string `s`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 100; lowercase letters only.

**Example:** `"xyzzaz"` → `1`: of `xyz`, `yzz`, `zza` and `zaz`, only `xyz` qualifies. `"aababcabc"` → `4`.
substrings-of-size-three-with-distinct-c.approach: For each i ≥ 2 check s[i], s[i−1], s[i−2] are pairwise different (or keep counts in a size-3 window).
substrings-of-size-three-with-distinct-c.trigger: "substrings of length k" with a per-window property.

maximum-sum-of-distinct-subarrays-with-l.title: Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K
maximum-sum-of-distinct-subarrays-with-l.statement: Among windows of length k whose elements are all distinct, return the largest sum (0 if none).
maximum-sum-of-distinct-subarrays-with-l.details:
**Task.** Look at every contiguous subarray of length exactly k whose elements are all different. Return the largest sum among them, or 0 if no such subarray exists.

**Input:** an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. **Output:** an integer (can exceed 32 bits).

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ k ≤ length ≤ 10⁵; 1 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[1, 5, 4, 2, 9, 9, 9]`, k = 3 → `15`, from `[4, 2, 9]`. The windows containing two 9s do not qualify. `[4, 4, 4]`, k = 3 → `0`.
maximum-sum-of-distinct-subarrays-with-l.pattern_name: Fixed window with a count map and a distinct counter
maximum-sum-of-distinct-subarrays-with-l.approach: Slide a window of size k keeping sum and a frequency map; the window qualifies when the number of distinct keys equals k.
maximum-sum-of-distinct-subarrays-with-l.trigger: "length k" + "all distinct" → fixed window + frequency map.

maximum-erasure-value.title: Maximum Erasure Value
maximum-erasure-value.statement: Pick one contiguous block with no repeated values; your score is its sum. Maximise the score.
maximum-erasure-value.details:
**Task.** Erase exactly one contiguous block of the array in which every value is different. You score the sum of the erased values. Return the maximum possible score.

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 10⁵; 1 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁴.

**Example:** `[4, 2, 4, 5, 6]` → `17`, from `[2, 4, 5, 6]`. `[5, 2, 1, 2, 5, 2, 1, 2, 5]` → `8`, from `[5, 2, 1]` or `[1, 2, 5]`.
maximum-erasure-value.pattern_name: Variable window with no repeats (sum instead of length)
maximum-erasure-value.approach: Exactly Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, but record the window sum instead of the length.

find-the-difference-of-two-arrays.title: Find the Difference of Two Arrays
find-the-difference-of-two-arrays.statement: Return the distinct values that appear only in the first array, and those that appear only in the second.
find-the-difference-of-two-arrays.details:
**Task.** Given two arrays, return two lists. The first holds the distinct values that occur in `nums1` but not in `nums2`; the second holds the distinct values that occur in `nums2` but not in `nums1`. Order within each list does not matter.

**Input:** integer arrays `nums1`, `nums2`. **Output:** a pair of integer lists.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ lengths ≤ 1000; −1000 ≤ values ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 3]`, `[2, 4, 6]` → `[[1, 3], [4, 6]]`. `[1, 2, 3, 3]`, `[1, 1, 2, 2]` → `[[3], []]`.
find-the-difference-of-two-arrays.approach: Build a set for each array; collect values of set A not in set B, and of set B not in set A.
find-the-difference-of-two-arrays.trigger: "present in one but not the other" → two hash sets.
